name: Mars Orange
lede: Mars orange is a reddish orange paint made synthetically from iron oxide, one of a family of eighteenth-century pigments named for the alchemists' planet-metal Mars.

sections.title: Why Mars
sections.body:
Mars orange belongs to the Mars pigments, a group of synthetic iron oxide colors with Mars black, brown, red, violet and yellow beside it [1][2]. The word Mars is alchemical: to alchemists Mars stood for iron, and Mars yellow, and the Mars colors derived from it, took the name in the eighteenth century by translating the Latin *crocus martius*, saffron of Mars [2]. Dictionaries define the color itself simply as a reddish orange [1].

The pigments were developed in the eighteenth century [2].

sections.title: How it was made
sections.body:
Makers precipitated iron salts (sulfates, chlorides, nitrates or acetates) with an alkali such as lime, caustic soda or potash [2]. That gave a yellow or yellow-brown paste, Mars yellow, which was washed free of acid [2]. Roasting the yellow oxidised it to iron(III) oxide and produced a range from oranges to reds, so the roast decided the shade [2].

One name is unsettled. Spanish ochre was sometimes a synonym for Mars orange, but Salter in 1869 tied it to a burnt yellow or Roman ochre instead [3]. French *laque minéral* was also used for orange oxide of iron, by Salter's account, and for a chromate-of-lead orange [4].

sections.title: In the paint box
sections.body:
Mars orange was a relatively new pure orange when William Holman Hunt used it in *The Awakening Conscience* in 1853, alongside chrome and strontium yellows, cobalt blue and emerald green [5]. Analysts have tentatively identified it in a paint box owned by Winslow Homer, labeled "rust orange" and mixed with calcite [2]. The Amsterdam firm Claus & Fritz (1841-1931) sold a version cut with a large amount of chalk, and the Belgian firm Blockx supplied one in which analysis found hematite, goethite and chrome orange [2]. Commercial Mars orange was therefore not a single fixed recipe [2].

To see it, look for a flat, slightly brick-leaning orange in nineteenth-century oils, closer to [[rust]] and [[burnt-orange]] than to [[vermilion]], which is brighter and redder, and nearer [[orange]] in family.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our library files Mars Orange with the painter's pigments [6]. It appears in Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, in ISCC-NBS block 37, and in Maerz & Paul's 1930 dictionary, which dates the name to 1835 [6]. Its nearest named neighbor is Rust, 5.5 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [6].

In the archive, 189 of 23,781 paintings carry this orange [7]. The strongest concentration is Indian: 40 of 721 Indian works show it, and 15 of 118 in the Pahari school [7]. The match is to the look, not to the Mars recipe [7]. The photographs are of aged paintings, so treat each match as approximate [7].

openers: The Mars in Mars orange is the alchemists' name for iron, and roasting a yellow iron paste produced the orange.
